Claude Code 2.1.94 Deep Dive: All 28 Changes Explained

Apr 8, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Scope: Claude Code Changelog 2.1.94 — all 28 changes Compared with: OpenAI Codex CLI, Google Gemini CLI

1. Added Amazon Bedrock Mantle Inference Support

Section titled “1. Added Amazon Bedrock Mantle Inference Support”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Amazon Mantle is AWS’s next-generation inference infrastructure layer, designed to replace traditional Bedrock inference endpoints with lower latency and higher throughput. Previously, Claude Code only supported standard Bedrock endpoints.

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  • Enterprise users running Claude Code on AWS who want better inference performance via Mantle
  • Set the environment variable: export CLAUDE_CODE_USE_MANTLE=1, then use Claude Code normally
  • Ideal for large-scale code generation tasks (like refactoring entire projects), as Mantle is optimized for long-context inference

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Requires AWS account with Mantle access enabled
  • May have compatibility requirements with existing Bedrock region configurations
  • The environment variable approach indicates this is still experimental

Version History

Section titled “Version History”
  • 2.1.92: Added interactive Bedrock setup wizard
  • 2.1.86: Improved prompt cache hit rates for Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry users
  • 2.1.84: Added capability detection override environment variables

Product Comparison

Section titled “Product Comparison”
  • Claude Code: Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, and now Mantle
  • Codex CLI: OpenAI API only, no direct cloud platform integration
  • Gemini CLI: Google AI API + Vertex AI, Gemini Code Assist Enterprise

Future Outlook

Section titled “Future Outlook”
  • Mantle may become the default inference path for Bedrock users once stable
  • Expect future versions to integrate Mantle into the interactive setup wizard

2. Default Effort Level Changed to High for Paid Users

Section titled “2. Default Effort Level Changed to High for Paid Users”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Claude Code introduced an effort concept (low/medium/high) controlling how deeply the model thinks. Previously all users defaulted to medium, but paid/enterprise users have higher quality expectations.

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  • Before: Team users refactoring complex code might get shallow analysis
  • Now: Default high effort produces more thorough, complete solutions
  • Still adjustable via /effort command for quick questions

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Only affects paid users: Free/individual subscription users unchanged
  • High effort means more token consumption and faster rate limit hits
  • /effort can switch anytime — not permanently locked

Version History

Section titled “Version History”
  • 2.1.80: Added effort frontmatter support
  • 2.1.78: Added agent frontmatter effort support
  • 2.1.76: Added /effort slash command

Product Comparison

Section titled “Product Comparison”
  • Claude Code: /effort with three levels, default changed this release
  • Codex CLI: No explicit effort control; relies on model selection
  • Gemini CLI: No direct equivalent; indirectly achieved via model routing (Flash vs Pro)

3. Compact Clickable Channel Header for Slack MCP Messages

Section titled “3. Compact Clickable Channel Header for Slack MCP Messages”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Claude Code integrates Slack via MCP. When sending messages to Slack channels, the UI now shows a clean, clickable channel header instead of raw JSON.

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  • Ask Claude Code to send a deployment notice to #dev-updates
  • Tool call area now shows a compact channel name with a clickable link
  • Much friendlier than seeing raw JSON parameters

4. New keep-coding-instructions Plugin Frontmatter Field

Section titled “4. New keep-coding-instructions Plugin Frontmatter Field”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Plugin output styles could override coding instructions from your configuration. The new field lets plugins declare “keep existing coding instructions.”

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  • A code style plugin injects formatting rules
  • With keep-coding-instructions: true, your existing rules won’t be overwritten
  • Prevents plugin conflicts from losing coding style instructions

5. Hook Support for Setting Session Titles

Section titled “5. Hook Support for Setting Session Titles”

Background

Section titled “Background”

The UserPromptSubmit hook can now control session titles via hookSpecificOutput.sessionTitle.

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  • Enterprise deployments: hooks automatically set titles matching ticket numbers

Version History

Section titled “Version History”
  • 2.1.85: Introduced conditional if field for hooks
  • 2.1.84: Added TaskCreated hook
  • 2.1.78: Added StopFailure hook

6. Plugin Skills Now Use Frontmatter Name Instead of Directory Name

Section titled “6. Plugin Skills Now Use Frontmatter Name Instead of Directory Name”

Background

Section titled “Background”

When plugins declare skills with "skills": ["./"], the invocation name was previously derived from the directory name. Different installation methods could produce different directory names, causing unstable identifiers.

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  • Plugin frontmatter declares name: lint-check
  • Before: Different names depending on installation method
  • Now: Always uses the frontmatter-defined name regardless of installation

7. Fixed Agents Appearing Stuck After Long Retry-After 429 Responses

Section titled “7. Fixed Agents Appearing Stuck After Long Retry-After 429 Responses”

Background

Section titled “Background”

When the API returned 429 with a long Retry-After (e.g., 300 seconds), Claude Code would silently wait with no feedback, making agents appear frozen.

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  • Running many parallel sub-agents in an enterprise environment
  • An agent hits rate limits with a “retry in 5 minutes” response
  • Before: Agent appears frozen for 5 minutes
  • Now: Error surfaces immediately; user decides to wait or cancel

Version History

Section titled “Version History”
  • 2.1.90: Fixed rate limit dialog infinite loop causing session crashes
  • 2.1.89: Fixed autocompact death loop on repeated context overflow
  • 2.1.79: Fixed enterprise users unable to retry after 429 errors

8. Fixed macOS Keychain Lock Causing Silent Login Failure

Section titled “8. Fixed macOS Keychain Lock Causing Silent Login Failure”

Background

Section titled “Background”

macOS stores OAuth credentials in Keychain. After system restarts, a locked keychain caused Claude Code to show only “Not logged in” with no diagnostic info.

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  • After macOS update and restart, Claude Code shows “Not logged in”
  • Now: Shows specific reason and claude doctor can diagnose and guide repair

9. Fixed Plugin Skill YAML Frontmatter Hooks Being Silently Ignored

Section titled “9. Fixed Plugin Skill YAML Frontmatter Hooks Being Silently Ignored”

A parsing bug caused hooks defined in plugin skill YAML frontmatter to be completely ignored without any warning. Now they’re correctly parsed and executed.

10. Fixed Plugin Hook Errors When Plugin Root Variable Was Not Set

Section titled “10. Fixed Plugin Hook Errors When Plugin Root Variable Was Not Set”

Plugin hooks referencing scripts via the plugin root path variable would fail with “No such file or directory” when the variable was unset. Now falls back to a reasonable default path.

11. Fixed Plugin Root Resolving to Marketplace Source Instead of Install Cache

Section titled “11. Fixed Plugin Root Resolving to Marketplace Source Instead of Install Cache”

For local-marketplace installed plugins, the root path variable incorrectly pointed to the original source directory rather than the installed cache. Only affects local-marketplace installations.

12. Fixed Repeated Diffs and Blank Pages in Long Session Scrollback

Section titled “12. Fixed Repeated Diffs and Blank Pages in Long Session Scrollback”

Long-running sessions with heavy diff output showed duplicate diffs and blank pages in the scrollback buffer.

Version History

Section titled “Version History”
  • 2.1.92: Fixed same message appearing in two positions during fullscreen scrolling
  • 2.1.89: Added flicker-free rendering mode
  • 2.1.85: Improved scrolling performance for large transcripts

13. Fixed Multiline Prompt Indentation Alignment

Section titled “13. Fixed Multiline Prompt Indentation Alignment”

Wrapped lines in multiline prompts were incorrectly indented under the ❯ caret instead of under the text content.

14. Fixed Shift+Space Inserting Literal “space” in Search Inputs

Section titled “14. Fixed Shift+Space Inserting Literal “space” in Search Inputs”

A keyboard event handling bug caused Shift+Space to insert the literal string “space” instead of a space character.

15. Fixed Hyperlinks Opening Two Browser Tabs in tmux + xterm.js

Section titled “15. Fixed Hyperlinks Opening Two Browser Tabs in tmux + xterm.js”

OSC 8 hyperlink sequences were double-processed when tmux ran inside xterm.js terminals (VS Code Terminal, Hyper, Tabby). Only affects the tmux + xterm.js combination.

16. Fixed Ghost Lines Accumulating During Alt-Screen Scrolling

Section titled “16. Fixed Ghost Lines Accumulating During Alt-Screen Scrolling”

Content height changes mid-scroll left un-cleared old lines that compounded over time, requiring Ctrl+L to refresh.

17. Fixed FORCE_HYPERLINK Environment Variable Ignored in settings.json

Section titled “17. Fixed FORCE_HYPERLINK Environment Variable Ignored in settings.json”

Hyperlink detection occurred before settings loaded, so the variable set via settings.json was ignored. Now settings environment variables load before detection.

18. Fixed Native Cursor Not Tracking Tab Selection in Dialogs (Accessibility)

Section titled “18. Fixed Native Cursor Not Tracking Tab Selection in Dialogs (Accessibility)”

The terminal’s native cursor didn’t follow tab selection in dialogs, affecting screen reader and magnifier users.

19. Fixed Bedrock Invocation of Sonnet 3.5 v2 Model ID

Section titled “19. Fixed Bedrock Invocation of Sonnet 3.5 v2 Model ID”

Sonnet 3.5 v2 uses a new us. prefixed inference profile ID that Claude Code wasn’t using. Only affects Bedrock users.

20. Fixed SDK/Print Mode Losing Partial Responses on Interruption

Section titled “20. Fixed SDK/Print Mode Losing Partial Responses on Interruption”

In claude -p mode, interrupting mid-stream now preserves the partial response in conversation history for --resume. Particularly important for CI/CD pipelines.

21. Improved Cross-Worktree Session Resume

Section titled “21. Improved Cross-Worktree Session Resume”

Previously, --resume for sessions from a different Git worktree only printed a cd command. Now it directly resumes with automatic context switching.

22. Fixed CJK and Multibyte Text Corruption in stream-json

Section titled “22. Fixed CJK and Multibyte Text Corruption in stream-json”

UTF-8 CJK characters split at chunk boundaries were decoded as U+FFFD replacement characters. Affects all stream-json usage (SDK, piped output).

Version History

Section titled “Version History”
  • 2.1.89: Fixed CJK/emoji dropped at 4KB boundaries in prompt history
  • 2.1.77: Fixed CJK characters visually overflowing at UI right edge

Product Comparison

Section titled “Product Comparison”
  • Claude Code: Continuous CJK fixes indicate a large Asian user base
  • Codex CLI: No similar CJK fix records
  • Gemini CLI: Some unicode crash fixes, but less frequent

23. [VS Code] Reduced Cold-Start Subprocess Overhead

Section titled “23. [VS Code] Reduced Cold-Start Subprocess Overhead”

Session startup now parallelizes or eliminates unnecessary subprocess initialization, reducing cold-open time.

24. [VS Code] Fixed Dropdown Menu Mouse/Keyboard Selection Conflict

Section titled “24. [VS Code] Fixed Dropdown Menu Mouse/Keyboard Selection Conflict”

Mouse hover events overrode keyboard selection when the cursor was over the dropdown list, causing wrong item selection.

25. [VS Code] Added Warning Banner for Unparseable settings.json

Section titled “25. [VS Code] Added Warning Banner for Unparseable settings.json”

When settings.json has JSON syntax errors, Claude Code previously fell back silently to defaults — potentially disabling permission rules (security concern). Now shows a clear warning banner.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

Release Characteristics

Section titled “Release Characteristics”

2.1.94 is primarily a stability and polish release. Among 28 changes:

  • New features: 4 (Mantle, effort defaults, Slack UI, plugin frontmatter)
  • Plugin/Hook system fixes: 5 (reflecting edge cases from rapid plugin ecosystem growth)
  • Terminal rendering fixes: 6 (scrollback, ghost lines, hyperlinks, CJK, etc.)
  • Platform compatibility: 3 (Bedrock, macOS keychain, tmux)
  • VS Code extension: 3
  • Other fixes: 7

Three-Product Comparison

Section titled “Three-Product Comparison”
  • Maturity: Claude Code is most mature (2.1.94 is extremely detailed); Codex CLI is newer; Gemini CLI is rapidly iterating
  • Plugin ecosystem: Claude Code is most complex (marketplace, hooks, skills); Codex CLI is simpler; Gemini CLI has an active extensions ecosystem
  • Terminal UI: Claude Code is highly complex (alt-screen, vim mode, voice); Codex CLI is minimal; Gemini CLI is catching up
  • Enterprise support: Claude Code is strongest (managed settings, multi-cloud); Codex CLI is OpenAI API only; Gemini CLI has Google Cloud + Vertex AI
  • CJK support: Claude Code invests heavily in fixes; others less so
  • Accessibility: Claude Code has screen reader/magnifier fix records; others don’t

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”
  1. Plugin system stabilization: Five plugin bug fixes indicate a shift from rapid iteration to stability
  2. Continued terminal rendering polish: Claude Code’s TUI complexity far exceeds competitors
  3. Multi-cloud inference: Mantle signals deeper infrastructure investment
  4. CJK/Internationalization: Continuous fixes across versions point to Asian market as a key growth area
  5. SDK/Automation: UTF-8 stream fixes and partial response preservation reflect growing CI/CD pipeline usage

  • Claude Code
  • AI Coding
  • Changelog

Claude Code 2.1.96 Changelog Deep Dive: Bedrock Auth Hotfix

Apr 8, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Release date: 2026-04-08 Changes: 1 (hotfix release)

The Fix: Bedrock Requests Failing with 403 “Authorization header is missing”

Section titled “The Fix: Bedrock Requests Failing with 403 “Authorization header is missing””

What Changed

Section titled “What Changed”

1. Background

Section titled “1. Background”

1.1 Bedrock Authentication Explained

Section titled “1.1 Bedrock Authentication Explained”

Claude Code supports three cloud backend options:

  • Anthropic API (direct connection, API Key auth)
  • Amazon Bedrock (calling Claude models through AWS infrastructure)
  • Google Vertex AI / Azure Foundry

The Bedrock path supports three authentication methods:

Auth MethodEnvironment VariableTypical Scenario
AWS SigV4 SigningCLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1 + standard AWS credentialsEC2 instance profiles, IAM roles, ~/.aws/credentials
Bearer TokenAWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK=<token>AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO), temporary tokens
Skip AuthCLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_BEDROCK_AUTH=1Gateway proxy scenarios where the gateway handles AWS auth

1.2 Root Cause: The Mantle Support Addition

Section titled “1.2 Root Cause: The Mantle Support Addition”

Version 2.1.94 introduced an important new feature: Amazon Bedrock powered by Mantle (CLAUDE_CODE_USE_MANTLE=1).

Mantle is a new Bedrock deployment mode from AWS. When adding Mantle support, the authentication module’s code paths were refactored — and this refactoring accidentally broke both the Bearer Token and Skip Auth paths.

Specifically, the refactoring likely changed the timing or conditional logic for how the HTTP client constructs the Authorization header, causing it to not be properly injected for non-standard SigV4 auth paths.

1.3 Impact Scope

Section titled “1.3 Impact Scope”

Based on GitHub Issues feedback:

  • #44910 — Bearer Token users started having issues from 2.1.92, worsened in 2.1.94
  • #44944 — Bedrock Bearer Token auth completely broken
  • #45128 — Even more serious: even after 2.1.96 fixed Bearer Token, standard SigV4 (instance profile) path still broken at the SDK level
  • #44899 — Mantle feature itself has no documentation

Affected user profiles:

  • Enterprise AWS Bedrock users (authenticating via SSO/Bearer Token)
  • Self-hosted LLM gateway users (relying on SKIP_BEDROCK_AUTH)
  • GitHub Actions users running automated code review in CI/CD pipelines

2. Use Cases and Examples

Section titled “2. Use Cases and Examples”

Scenario 1: Enterprise SSO Authentication (Bearer Token)

Section titled “Scenario 1: Enterprise SSO Authentication (Bearer Token)”

Typical users: Enterprise development teams obtaining temporary credentials through their company’s AWS SSO portal, not using long-term IAM keys.

Scenario 2: LLM Gateway Proxy (Skip Auth)

Section titled “Scenario 2: LLM Gateway Proxy (Skip Auth)”

Typical users: DevOps teams managing AI API calls through a unified gateway for auditing, rate limiting, and cost allocation.

Scenario 3: CI/CD Automation (GitHub Actions)

Section titled “Scenario 3: CI/CD Automation (GitHub Actions)”

This scenario may still be broken in 2.1.96 — #45128 reports the SDK 0.2.96 SigV4 path is still broken.

Scenario 4: settings.json Configuration (Non-Environment Variable)

Section titled “Scenario 4: settings.json Configuration (Non-Environment Variable)”

Gotcha: #44910 points out a potential race condition — env injection from settings.json may take effect after the Bedrock client constructor reads process.env, causing the token to be missed even with correct configuration.

3. Important Notes

Section titled “3. Important Notes”

3.1 Verify Your Auth Path Before Upgrading to 2.1.96

Section titled “3.1 Verify Your Auth Path Before Upgrading to 2.1.96”
Your Auth MethodFixed in 2.1.96?Recommendation
Bearer Token (AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK)✅ FixedUpgrade directly
Skip Auth (CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_BEDROCK_AUTH)✅ FixedUpgrade directly
Standard SigV4 (IAM keys/instance profiles)⚠️ May still be brokenTest before upgrading, watch #45128
Mantle (CLAUDE_CODE_USE_MANTLE=1)❓ UnknownNo docs, use with caution

3.2 Rollback Options

Section titled “3.2 Rollback Options”

If issues persist after upgrading:

3.3 Verifying Auth Works

Section titled “3.3 Verifying Auth Works”

3.4 Environment Variable Priority Gotcha

Section titled “3.4 Environment Variable Priority Gotcha”

Environment variables > ~/.claude/settings.json env config. If both are set, shell environment variables take precedence. But settings.json injection timing may have race condition issues (see Scenario 4).

4. Version History Timeline

Section titled “4. Version History Timeline”
VersionBedrock-Related ChangesStatus
2.1.84Added interactive Bedrock setup wizard; added model support env vars✅
2.1.86Improved prompt cache hit rate for Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry users✅
2.1.91Last version with fully working Bedrock auth✅ Stable
2.1.92Added forceRemoteSettingsRefresh strategy; Bearer Token issues reported⚠️ Suspected regression
2.1.94Added Mantle support; fixed Sonnet 3.5 v2 Bedrock calls; changed default effort❌ Regression confirmed
2.1.96Fixed Bearer Token and Skip Auth path 403 errors🔧 Partial fix

Key Code Path Evolution

Section titled “Key Code Path Evolution”

5. Competitor Comparison

Section titled “5. Competitor Comparison”

5.1 OpenAI Codex CLI

Section titled “5.1 OpenAI Codex CLI”
  • Cloud backends: OpenAI API only, no native AWS/GCP/Azure integration
  • Auth methods: Single API Key
  • Enterprise deployment: Relies on Azure OpenAI Service, simpler config path
  • Comparison: Claude Code’s multi-cloud support is far more complex than Codex, with higher regression risk but more flexible enterprise deployment options

5.2 Google Gemini CLI

Section titled “5.2 Google Gemini CLI”
  • Cloud backends: Gemini API + Vertex AI
  • Auth methods: Google Cloud Application Default Credentials (ADC), simpler than AWS multi-path auth
  • Similar issues: Gemini CLI has also experienced Vertex AI auth regressions, but Google’s unified ADC model reduces the probability
  • Comparison: AWS auth methods are far more complex than Google ADC, giving Claude Code more auth permutations to handle

5.3 Summary Comparison

Section titled “5.3 Summary Comparison”
DimensionClaude CodeCodex CLIGemini CLI
Cloud backends4 (Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry/Mantle)1 (OpenAI/Azure)2 (Gemini API/Vertex)
Auth paths6+ (API Key, SigV4, Bearer, SSO, Skip, Mantle)1-22-3
Regression riskHigh (many paths, combinatorial explosion)LowMedium
Hotfix speedFast (2.1.94→2.1.96 in days)——
Enterprise depthDeep (gateway proxy, managed settings)ShallowMedium

6. Future Trends

Section titled “6. Future Trends”

6.1 Short-term (1-3 months)

Section titled “6.1 Short-term (1-3 months)”
  • SigV4 path fix: #45128 shows SDK-level SigV4 issues remain, expected fix in next version
  • Mantle documentation: #44899 requires completing documentation pages, high-priority docs debt
  • Auth module refactor: Two consecutive Bedrock auth regressions indicate architectural fragility, expect a more systematic refactor

6.2 Medium-term (3-6 months)

Section titled “6.2 Medium-term (3-6 months)”
  • Auth test matrix: Multi-path auth needs comprehensive integration test coverage, expected to join CI
  • Unified auth layer abstraction: Current Bedrock auth methods are scattered across different code paths, may be unified into an AuthProvider interface pattern
  • Mantle maturation: As AWS’s new Bedrock deployment mode, expect it to gradually gain documentation and test coverage on par with standard Bedrock

6.3 Long-term trends

Section titled “6.3 Long-term trends”
  • Multi-cloud auth standardization: As Claude Code supports 4 cloud backends, auth logic complexity will keep growing. Plugin-based auth architecture may emerge
  • Auth regression detection: CI may add “auth smoke tests” to automatically verify all cloud backend paths before each release
  • Gateway ecosystem maturation: Features like CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_BEDROCK_AUTH show the enterprise gateway ecosystem is growing, with more elegant gateway integrations likely ahead

7. Conclusion

Section titled “7. Conclusion”

2.1.96 is a pure hotfix release — it fixes just one bug, but behind that bug lies an engineering problem worth paying attention to:

Core lesson: When a product’s auth paths grow from 1 to 6+, each new path (like Mantle) can break existing ones. This isn’t unique to Anthropic — any multi-cloud product faces this challenge.

Recommendations for users:

  1. If you use Bearer Token or Skip Auth → Upgrade to 2.1.96
  2. If you use standard SigV4 → Wait and watch #45128
  3. If you want to try Mantle → Wait for documentation
  4. Regardless, pin your Claude Code version in CI/CD — don’t use @latest

Configuring Claude CLI as a Model in openclaw: asdf Shim Conflicts and Billing Changes

Apr 8, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Configuring multiple model providers in OpenClaw is a common need. This post documents the full process of adding Claude CLI (via OAuth authentication) as a fallback model, including two major issues encountered along the way.

Background

Section titled “Background”

OpenClaw supports multi-model configurations with a primary model and fallback chain. The goal was to add claude-cli/claude-opus-4-6 as a fallback model, calling the Anthropic API through the local Claude Code CLI’s OAuth authentication.

Configuration Steps

Section titled “Configuration Steps”

1. Add Auth Profile

Section titled “1. Add Auth Profile”

Register Claude CLI’s OAuth authentication:

This command:

  • Reads OAuth credentials from the Claude CLI keychain
  • Creates a claude-cli provider in openclaw.json
  • Adds an authentication profile (OAuth type)

Note: Don’t add --set-default — this is only intended as a fallback model.

2. Clean Up Unnecessary Models

Section titled “2. Clean Up Unnecessary Models”

The command adds several models by default (sonnet, opus-4-5, haiku, etc.). Remove everything except the desired claude-cli/claude-opus-4-6.

3. Final Model Configuration

Section titled “3. Final Model Configuration”

Claude CLI sits at the end of the fallback chain — only used when all other models fail.

Pitfalls Encountered

Section titled “Pitfalls Encountered”

Pitfall 1: asdf Shim Conflict

Section titled “Pitfall 1: asdf Shim Conflict”

Symptom: Selecting claude-cli/claude-opus-4-6 caused automatic fallback to other models.

Log error:

Root cause: Two Claude CLI installations existed on the system:

  • ~/.asdf/installs/nodejs/*/bin/claude — old version (installed via npm global)
  • ~/.local/bin/claude — new version (official standalone install)

The Gateway process looked up the claude command through the asdf shim, but the working directory’s .tool-versions didn’t specify the corresponding Node.js version, causing asdf to intercept and error out.

Fix: Remove the old claude from asdf so the shim no longer intercepts:

After the fix, the Gateway correctly found ~/.local/bin/claude (new version).

Lesson learned: When using asdf to manage Node.js versions, globally installed npm CLI tools create shims. If you later install the same command via a standalone installer, the asdf shim takes priority and intercepts the call, causing path resolution failures.

Pitfall 2: Anthropic Billing Policy Change

Section titled “Pitfall 2: Anthropic Billing Policy Change”

After fixing the asdf issue, a 402 error appeared:

Anthropic has separated third-party app usage (like Claude Code CLI) from subscription plan limits. You need to claim credits at claude.ai/settings/usage before the model can be used.

This is a platform policy change, not a configuration issue.

Current Limitations

Section titled “Current Limitations”
LimitationDetails
Billing credits not activatedMust claim credits at claude.ai/settings/usage
OAuth token expiryTokens expire and need periodic refresh
Depends on local Claude CLIRequires ~/.local/bin/claude to be executable and authenticated
200k context windowCompared to billing-proxy’s 1M context, claude-cli is limited to 200k

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

claude-cli/claude-opus-4-6 has been successfully configured as a fallback model, though it’s temporarily unusable due to Anthropic’s billing policy change. The main pitfall was the asdf shim conflict with the standalone Claude CLI installation — a common issue with Node.js version managers. Similar problems can occur with nvm and volta.

The takeaway: keep a single installation source for each command to avoid shim and PATH priority conflicts.

OpenClaw 2026.4.7 Bug Fixes Deep Analysis

Apr 8, 2026
Vibe Sparking

This document provides a deep analysis of all 71 bug fixes in the OpenClaw 2026.4.7 release.

1. CLI/infer: Align Inference Behavior with Actual Runtime Execution

Section titled “1. CLI/infer: Align Inference Behavior with Actual Runtime Execution”

Fix Summary

Section titled “Fix Summary”

Fixed multiple inconsistencies between openclaw infer CLI command and the actual runtime, including TTS overrides, profile-aware gateway TTS preferences, transcription prompt/language overrides, image output MIME/extension mismatch, web-search fallback, and agent vs CLI web-search behavior drift.

Background

Section titled “Background”

openclaw infer as a standalone CLI inference command should produce results identical to the agent runtime. However, as features evolved, the two paths diverged: TTS configuration didn’t read profile-level preferences, transcription ignored user-specified prompt and language parameters, image generation MIME types didn’t match file extensions (e.g., returning PNG data but labeling as .jpg), and web-search had fallback logic in the agent but not in CLI. The root cause was insufficient code sharing between infer and agent paths.

Impact

Section titled “Impact”
  • Voice generated via openclaw infer --tts differed from agent conversations
  • Image file extensions didn’t match actual content, causing viewer failures
  • Web-search results differed between CLI and agent, breaking automation scripts

2. Plugins/media: Merge Capability Plugin IDs into Allowlist

Section titled “2. Plugins/media: Merge Capability Plugin IDs into Allowlist”

Fix Summary

Section titled “Fix Summary”

When plugins.allow is set, the capability fallback logic now merges built-in capability plugin IDs into the allow list, so OpenAI-compatible STT and other media providers load without explicitly declaring openai in plugins.allow. (#62205)

Background

Section titled “Background”

OpenClaw’s plugin security model lets users restrict loadable plugins via plugins.allow. But built-in “capability plugins” (like STT providers) are core platform features, not third-party plugins. The previous implementation only merged IDs from plugins.entries, missing built-in capability plugin IDs.

OpenClaw 2026.4.8 Deep Dive: A Fix-by-Fix Analysis

Apr 8, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Analysis based on source code commit 5982f2e and its preceding patch chain

Table of Contents

Section titled “Table of Contents”
  1. Telegram/setup: Sidecar Loading Fix
  2. Bundled channels/setup: Cross-Channel Sidecar Unified Fix
  3. Bundled plugins: Version Compatibility Metadata Alignment
  4. Agents/progress: update_plan Tool Improvements
  5. Agents/exec: Aligning Default Exec Policy with Runtime Behavior

1. Telegram/setup: Sidecar Loading Fix

Section titled “1. Telegram/setup: Sidecar Loading Fix”

Background

Section titled “Background”

OpenClaw uses a bundled channel architecture — each messaging channel (Telegram, Slack, etc.) is packaged as a built-in plugin under the dist/extensions/ directory. Starting from 2026.4.5, the build system introduced sidecar entry files (e.g., setup-entry.ts, secret-contract-api.ts) so that the dist/ artifacts after npm installation no longer need to reach into src/ subdirectories to load modules.

However, the Telegram channel’s entry files still referenced ./src/channel.setup.js and ./src/secret-contract.js — paths that exist in the development environment but not in npm-published build artifacts.

The Fix

Section titled “The Fix”

A new setup-plugin-api.ts was also added as a narrow export entry:

Who’s Affected

Section titled “Who’s Affected”

Every user who installed via npm install -g or brew install hits this bug. Typical symptoms:

  • Gateway startup throws Cannot find module 'dist/extensions/telegram/src/channel.setup.js'
  • Telegram bot fails to start; Telegram configuration step fails during the setup wizard

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Only affects npm-published builds; running directly from git source is unaffected
  • This regression was introduced in 2026.4.7 (sidecar refactor didn’t fully cover Telegram)
  • Upgrading to 2026.4.8 and restarting the gateway resolves the issue

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
ProductChannel Loading Mechanism
OpenClawBundled extension + sidecar entries, generated at compile time
NanoClawHardcoded WhatsApp (Baileys), no plugin system
NanobotDirect Python imports, no bundled build complexity
ZeroClawRust trait static compilation, no runtime module loading issues

As the only large-scale TypeScript monorepo architecture, OpenClaw faces far greater module resolution and bundling complexity than other products. These sidecar issues are fundamentally a systemic problem of Node.js ESM + inconsistent build artifact paths.

2. Bundled channels/setup: Cross-Channel Sidecar Unified Fix

Section titled “2. Bundled channels/setup: Cross-Channel Sidecar Unified Fix”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Same root cause as the Telegram issue: all bundled channels had the same ./src/secret-contract.js reference problem in both their runtime entries and setup wizard entries.

A total of 10 channels were affected: BlueBubbles, Feishu, Google Chat, IRC, Matrix, Mattermost, Microsoft Teams, Nextcloud Talk, Slack, and Zalo.

The Fix

Section titled “The Fix”

All channels’ secrets.specifier was uniformly changed from ./src/secret-contract.js to ./secret-contract-api.js, with the channelSecrets export added to each channel.

This involved batch modifications across 34 files, all following the same pattern:

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • A regression test bundled-plugin-build-entries.test.ts was added to the build system to prevent similar oversights in the future
  • OpenClaw is the only open-source AI agent framework supporting 10+ messaging platforms, and this breadth brings a unique level of maintenance complexity

3. Bundled plugins: Version Compatibility Metadata Alignment

Section titled “3. Bundled plugins: Version Compatibility Metadata Alignment”

Background

Section titled “Background”

OpenClaw’s bundled plugins declare a compatible version number in their metadata. The gateway checks version compatibility at startup, and mismatched plugins are skipped.

During the preparation for 2026.4.8, some bundled plugins still had their version metadata stuck on older version numbers, preventing them from loading.

The Fix

Section titled “The Fix”

The build script now synchronizes all bundled plugin compatibility version numbers with the release version.

Who’s Affected

Section titled “Who’s Affected”

This issue can be triggered with every version upgrade. If channels or providers “disappear” after an upgrade, it’s likely a version metadata mismatch.

Version History

Section titled “Version History”
VersionEvent
2026.3.29Node minor version upgrade caused plugin hash changes
2026.4.5Major config schema overhaul, openclaw doctor --fix migration
2026.4.7Many new bundled plugins
2026.4.8Version metadata aligned with release version

4. Agents/progress: update_plan Tool Improvements

Section titled “4. Agents/progress: update_plan Tool Improvements”

Background

Section titled “Background”

update_plan is an experimental tool OpenClaw introduced for OpenAI models, allowing them to report progress and plan steps during long-running tasks. Previous issues:

  • No opt-out: OpenAI users couldn’t disable it even with planTool=false
  • Oversized return values: Each call returned the full plan JSON, wasting tokens

The Fix

Section titled “The Fix”

Logic change:

Leaner return values:

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  1. GPT-5/Codex users: Enabled by default; UI displays structured progress during long tasks
  2. OpenAI users who don’t want plans: Set planTool: false to disable
  3. Non-OpenAI users: Set planTool: true to manually enable

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • The leaner return values save approximately 50–200 tokens per call, yielding significant cost savings in long sessions
  • OpenClaw leads in agent observability; update_plan + structured progress events is a unique feature

5. Agents/exec: Aligning Default Exec Policy with Runtime Behavior

Section titled “5. Agents/exec: Aligning Default Exec Policy with Runtime Behavior”

Background

Section titled “Background”

OpenClaw’s exec tool has three configuration dimensions:

  • host: Where the command runs (gateway, sandbox, node, auto)
  • security: Security policy (full/allowlist/deny)
  • ask: Approval mode (on-miss/always/off)

The hardcoded defaults were security: "deny" + ask: "on-miss", but actual runtime behavior differed:

  • On Gateway/Node: Actually full + off (approval system serves as the safety net)
  • On Sandbox: Actually deny + off (the sandbox itself provides isolation)

The model’s understanding was inconsistent with actual behavior.

The Fix

Section titled “The Fix”

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • This fix does not change actual execution behavior — only what default policy is reported to the model
  • This is an agent cognitive accuracy fix that indirectly improves exec tool usage rates and accuracy
  • OpenClaw’s exec security model is the most flexible yet also the most complex; this fix illustrates a common issue in complex configuration systems: semantic drift of default values

6. Slack: Socket Mode Proxy Support

Section titled “6. Slack: Socket Mode Proxy Support”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Enterprise environments often require all outbound traffic to go through an HTTP proxy. Slack’s Socket Mode uses long-lived WebSocket connections, but OpenClaw’s Slack client did not read proxy settings when creating WebSocket connections.

The Fix

Section titled “The Fix”
  1. Unified proxy URL resolution: Replaced with OpenClaw’s shared resolveEnvHttpProxyUrl("https")
  2. Fixed NO_PROXY parsing: Now supports space-separated values, *.domain wildcards, and empty-value override semantics
  3. Applied to Socket Mode: Proxy is now used for both REST API and WebSocket connections

Use Case

Section titled “Use Case”

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Contributed by a community contributor
  • Proxy settings follow standard HTTPS_PROXY / HTTP_PROXY / NO_PROXY environment variables

7. Slack/actions: downloadFile Token Fix

Section titled “7. Slack/actions: downloadFile Token Fix”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Slack’s downloadFile action requires a valid bot token. OpenClaw supports SecretRef (referencing tokens from external secret management systems). However, on certain code paths, the code would re-read the raw config, retrieving the SecretRef string instead of the actual resolved token.

The Fix

Section titled “The Fix”

The already-resolved readToken from the action runtime is now passed directly to downloadFile, rather than letting it re-read from the config.

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Contributed by a community contributor
  • Users with plaintext tokens are unaffected by this bug
  • SecretRef is an advanced OpenClaw feature for integrating with secret management systems like 1Password and HashiCorp Vault

8. Network/fetch guard: Skipping DNS Pinning in Trusted Proxy Mode

Section titled “8. Network/fetch guard: Skipping DNS Pinning in Trusted Proxy Mode”

Background

Section titled “Background”

OpenClaw’s SSRF Guard performs DNS pinning when agents make external requests (resolving the IP first and checking whether it’s a private address). However, in proxy-only sandbox environments where there’s no direct DNS resolution capability, DNS pinning fails.

The Fix

Section titled “The Fix”

A fallback was also added: when no proxy environment variables are configured, it falls back to standard DNS pinning.

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Contributed by a community contributor
  • Does not reduce security: In trusted proxy mode, the security policy is “trust the proxy to perform security checks”
  • OpenClaw’s SSRF guard is the most granular among all similar products, supporting multiple network topologies

SSRF Guard History

Section titled “SSRF Guard History”

2026.4.7Cross-origin redirect body stripping, browser SSRF redirect blocking
2026.4.8Trusted proxy mode skips DNS pinning

9. Comparison with Similar Open-Source Products

Architectural Takeaways from Each Fix

Section titled “Architectural Takeaways from Each Fix”
  1. Sidecar/bundling issues (Fix 1–3): TypeScript + ESM specific; Rust/Go compile to a single binary and don’t have these problems — this is the cost of the architectural choice
  2. Plan tool (Fix 4): A unique OpenClaw agent observability feature
  3. Exec default policy (Fix 5): The complexity cost of a three-dimensional configuration system
  4. Proxy support (Fix 6, 8): An enterprise deployment necessity; OpenClaw and ZeroClaw have the best support
  5. SecretRef (Fix 7): An advanced secret management feature unique to OpenClaw

10. Future Evolution Trends

Short Term (2026 Q2–Q3)

  1. Build system stabilization: The sidecar fixes indicate the bundling/module system is still maturing; expect further automation of bundled plugin entry validation and version synchronization
  2. Network configuration simplification: Three network-related fixes suggest a unified network configuration layer is coming
  3. Exec security model convergence: Expect simplification into fewer modes with reduced configuration dimensions

Medium Term (2026 Q4 — 2027)

OpenClaw Upgrade Troubleshooting - From 2026.4.5 to 2026.4.8

Apr 8, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Background

Section titled “Background”

I was running OpenClaw 2026.4.5 and wanted to upgrade to the latest version. What should have been a simple npm i -g turned into a multi-step debugging session involving PATH conflicts, packaging bugs, and version constraint mismatches.

Problem 1: npm Install Doesn’t Update the Version

Section titled “Problem 1: npm Install Doesn’t Update the Version”

After installing openclaw@2026.4.7, the version still showed 2026.4.5. The clue was in which openclaw:

Root Cause

Section titled “Root Cause”

I had two Node.js installations on the system:

  • asdf (Node v24.9.0): npm global prefix at ~/.asdf/installs/nodejs/24.9.0/
  • Homebrew: npm global prefix at /opt/homebrew/

The npm i -g openclaw@2026.4.7 command used asdf’s npm and installed to the asdf path. But /opt/homebrew/bin/openclaw (from a previous curl | bash install) came first in PATH, shadowing the new version.

Fix

Section titled “Fix”

Lesson Learned

Section titled “Lesson Learned”

When you have multiple Node.js version managers (asdf, nvm, Homebrew), always check which npm is actually running your install and where the binary resolves. The curl | bash installer for OpenClaw uses Homebrew’s npm by default on macOS, which can conflict with asdf-managed Node.

Problem 2: Telegram Plugin Packaging Bug in 2026.4.7

Section titled “Problem 2: Telegram Plugin Packaging Bug in 2026.4.7”

After resolving the PATH issue, I decided to install via Homebrew’s npm directly:

Running openclaw doctor --fix revealed a config read failure:

Root Cause

Section titled “Root Cause”

The setup-entry.js in the Telegram extension referenced source paths (./src/channel.setup.js) instead of the compiled dist paths (./setup-plugin-api.js). The src/ directory was not included in the published npm package. This was a build/bundler bug in the 2026.4.7 release.

Problem 3: Version 2026.4.7-1 Fixed Telegram But Broke Everything Else

Section titled “Problem 3: Version 2026.4.7-1 Fixed Telegram But Broke Everything Else”

Upgraded to the patch release:

The Telegram setup-entry.js was fixed, now correctly referencing ./setup-plugin-api.js. However, openclaw doctor --fix showed 22 plugins failing:

Root Cause

Section titled “Root Cause”

The bundled plugin manifests (package.json) inside the 2026.4.7-1 package had their engines.openclaw field set to >=2026.4.8, making them incompatible with the host version they were shipped with. Another packaging oversight.

Solution: Install 2026.4.8

Section titled “Solution: Install 2026.4.8”

Checked npm for available versions:

2026.4.8 was available and resolved all issues:

All 22 plugins now load correctly, and openclaw doctor --fix runs cleanly.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
VersionStatusIssue
2026.4.5✅ WorkingStarting point
2026.4.7❌ BrokenTelegram setup-entry.js references missing src/ paths
2026.4.7-1❌ Broken22 bundled plugins require >=2026.4.8
2026.4.8✅ WorkingAll issues resolved

Takeaways

Section titled “Takeaways”
  1. Multiple Node.js managers create PATH conflicts. Always verify which <binary> and npm prefix -g match your expectations.
  2. The curl | bash installer for OpenClaw uses Homebrew’s npm on macOS, which creates binaries at /opt/homebrew/bin/. If you later use asdf or nvm, these stale symlinks will shadow your new installs.
  3. Patch versions can have packaging bugs. When a point release doesn’t work, check if a newer version exists before spending time on workarounds.
  4. openclaw doctor --fix is your friend for diagnosing config and plugin issues after upgrades.

Shipping a Full CI/CD Pipeline Through OpenClaw Chat: 10 Iterations, 9 Bugs, One Green Run

Apr 8, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Intro

Section titled “Intro”

This post documents a complete CI/CD deployment flow driven through the OpenClaw chat interface. No manually opening a terminal, no hand-editing YAML, and no clicking through GitHub Actions pages to debug jobs. Nearly everything happened in chat, using natural language to drive OpenClaw through the work.

The project was openclaw Manager (ocm), a multi-instance OpenClaw cluster management tool that includes:

  • A cross-platform CLI for 5 targets
  • An Electron Desktop app for macOS, Windows, and Linux
  • A containerized Server + Web stack
  • An Astro website deployed to Cloudflare Pages

The target was simple: run git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin v0.1.0, then let automation handle cross-platform builds, packaging, Docker pushes, and GitHub Release publishing.

Round 1: Generate the Release Workflow

Section titled “Round 1: Generate the Release Workflow”

OpenClaw first inspected package.json, electron-builder.yml, and the Dockerfile to understand the project layout, then generated a complete GitHub Actions workflow in one pass.

The core jobs looked like this:

The distribution model was also clean:

  • Desktop users get the Desktop app, which bundles server, web, and CLI pieces
  • Command-line users get CLI binaries
  • Self-hosted users get a Docker image

After that, OpenClaw committed the workflow, pushed the branch, created a tag, triggered CI, and even created a cron monitor to report status every two minutes.

Round 2: All Desktop Builds Fail

Section titled “Round 2: All Desktop Builds Fail”

In the first run, the CLI and Docker jobs passed quickly, but all three Desktop builds failed.

The logs exposed two classic packaging issues:

  1. apps/desktop/package.json was missing description and author
  2. The Electron version was declared as ^33.0.0 instead of a fixed version, which broke electron-builder’s version detection

The fixes were straightforward:

  • Add description and author
  • Pin electron and electron-builder to exact versions

This was not really a product bug. It was a packaging metadata problem surfacing in CI.

Round 3: Bun and electron-builder Fight Each Other

Section titled “Round 3: Bun and electron-builder Fight Each Other”

Once the desktop bundle step passed, electron-builder failed again while installing production dependencies. The error was strange at first glance: Node.js was trying to execute the bun binary as if it were JavaScript.

The root cause was that electron-builder detected bun in PATH and incorrectly tried to use it during dependency installation.

The fix was small but important:

  1. Remove bun from PATH before the electron-builder step
  2. Make sure a web build failure would not block desktop packaging

Example:

Round 4: npm Does Not Understand workspace:*

Section titled “Round 4: npm Does Not Understand workspace:*”

After bun was removed, electron-builder fell back to npm, which immediately hit another issue:

This is a familiar monorepo trap. workspace:* is fine for bun or pnpm, but npm does not understand it.

More importantly, those dependencies had already been bundled earlier, so electron-builder did not need to reinstall them at all.

The final fix had two parts:

  1. Add npmRebuild: false to electron-builder.yml
  2. Remove unnecessary dependencies from the desktop package manifest

Rounds 5 and 6: electron-builder Edge Cases

Section titled “Rounds 5 and 6: electron-builder Edge Cases”

The next two issues were both very typical electron-builder traps.

1. Missing repository metadata

Section titled “1. Missing repository metadata”

electron-builder could not infer repository information from .git/config, so the repository field had to be added explicitly in package.json:

2. The publish: never semantic trap

Section titled “2. The publish: never semantic trap”

Writing publish: never inside electron-builder.yml looks reasonable, but electron-builder interprets it like a publisher name and tries to load a non-existent electron-publisher-never module.

The correct approach is not a config change. It is a CLI flag:

Small detail, big time sink.

Round 7: Everything Builds, but Release Still Fails

Section titled “Round 7: Everything Builds, but Release Still Fails”

At this stage, all build jobs passed for the first time:

  • build-cli ✅
  • build-docker ✅
  • build-desktop-mac ✅
  • build-desktop-win ✅
  • build-desktop-linux ✅

But the release job still failed because artifact downloads timed out. The reason was simple: desktop artifacts were too large, and downloading everything in one shot was unreliable.

The fix was to download artifacts one by one rather than in a single bulk step.

Not flashy, just more resilient.

Round 8: Cross-Repo GitHub Release Returns 404

Section titled “Round 8: Cross-Repo GitHub Release Returns 404”

Once builds and artifact downloads were working, another subtle problem surfaced:

  • gh release create --repo other/repo returned 404
  • GH_TOKEN had already been set

The real issue was token precedence. Inside GitHub Actions, the gh CLI prefers GITHUB_TOKEN, and that default token only has access to the current repository.

The effective fix was to override both variables in the job environment:

This turned out to be one of the most important lessons in the whole pipeline.

Round 10: Fully Green

Section titled “Round 10: Fully Green”

After 10 iterations, the workflow finally went fully green:

The final outputs included:

  • A public GitHub Release page
  • CLI binaries for 5 platforms
  • Desktop installers for macOS, Windows, and Linux
  • Docker images at ghcr.io/vs-openclaw/ocm-server
  • A SHA256SUMS.txt checksum file

In total, 9 bugs were fixed along the way:

  1. Missing metadata in package.json
  2. Unpinned Electron version
  3. Bun conflicting with electron-builder
  4. npm not supporting workspace:*
  5. Missing repository metadata
  6. Incorrect use of publish: never
  7. Artifact bulk download timeout
  8. GITHUB_TOKEN taking precedence over GH_TOKEN
  9. Intermittent Linux AppImage 502 failures requiring release-job fault tolerance

What OpenClaw Actually Saved

Section titled “What OpenClaw Actually Saved”

The biggest win here was not “AI can write YAML.” It was how much shorter the debug loop became:

  • pull logs
  • identify root cause
  • patch code or workflow
  • commit and push
  • re-trigger CI
  • monitor progress via cron

Doing that manually means constant window switching, copying logs around, searching errors, editing files, and triggering jobs again. Over 10 iterations, that operational overhead adds up fast.

Inside OpenClaw, those steps can be chained together in conversation, which makes the whole loop faster and harder to break.

Key Takeaways

Section titled “Key Takeaways”

The most valuable lessons from this run were:

  1. Bun monorepos plus electron-builder are a risky combination. Handle npm compatibility and rebuild behavior early.
  2. GitHub Actions token precedence is surprisingly tricky. For cross-repo releases, override both GH_TOKEN and GITHUB_TOKEN.
  3. electron-builder YAML config and CLI flags are not always semantically equivalent, especially around publish: never.
  4. Release jobs should be fault tolerant. One flaky platform should not block the whole release pipeline.
  5. Chat-driven agents are a strong fit for CI debugging, because they compress the loop of reading logs, analyzing, patching, and retrying.

One-Line Summary

Section titled “One-Line Summary”

Four hours, 10 CI rounds, 9 bugs, zero manual terminal work, and a fully working cross-platform release pipeline.

If you are already using OpenClaw, one of the best ways to push it beyond demos is to bring it into real delivery workflows. CI/CD, with its fast feedback loops and repetitive iteration, is exactly the kind of environment where an agent can pull real weight.

Matt Pocock Skills Deep Dive: 17 AI Agent Skills Fully Dissected

Vibe Sparking

Source: mattpocock/skills Survey date: 2026-04-07 Total: 17 skills covering planning, development, tooling, and writing

I. Planning & Design

Section titled “I. Planning & Design”

1. write-a-prd

Section titled “1. write-a-prd”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/write-a-prd
  • What it does: Generates a complete Product Requirements Document (PRD) through interactive interviews + codebase exploration, submitted as a GitHub Issue
  • Core workflow:
    1. Gather detailed problem and solution descriptions from the user
    2. Explore the codebase to verify current state
    3. Drill into every decision branch until consensus is reached
    4. Design module boundaries, pursuing “deep modules” (small interfaces, large implementations)
    5. Generate PRD from template (problem statement, solution, user stories, implementation decisions, module design)
  • Use cases:
    • Want to add a notification system but haven’t thought through the details — run this skill to turn vague ideas into structured documentation
    • Replace “let’s have a meeting to discuss” when kicking off new features

2. prd-to-plan

Section titled “2. prd-to-plan”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/prd-to-plan
  • What it does: Breaks a PRD into multi-phase implementation plans using tracer bullet vertical slices, output to ./plans/
  • Core workflow:
    1. Confirm PRD is in context
    2. Explore codebase to understand architecture
    3. Identify durable architectural decisions (routing, schema, auth patterns, etc.)
    4. Split by vertical slices — each phase cuts through all integration layers (schema → API → UI → tests)
    5. Confirm granularity with user, iterate until satisfied
    6. Write to ./plans/ Markdown files
  • Use cases:
    • PRD is ready, need to schedule and phase the implementation
    • Ensure every development phase can demo independently, not “it only works on the last day”

3. prd-to-issues

Section titled “3. prd-to-issues”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/prd-to-issues
  • What it does: Splits a PRD into independently claimable GitHub Issues, annotated with dependencies and HITL/AFK types
  • Core workflow:
    1. Get PRD (GitHub Issue number)
    2. Optionally explore codebase
    3. Split into vertical slices, label HITL (needs human decision) / AFK (can be done autonomously)
    4. Confirm granularity, dependencies, and categories with user
    5. Create GitHub Issues in dependency order
  • Use cases:
    • Multi-person team collaboration, turning large requirements into assignable tickets
    • Let AI agents autonomously execute AFK-type issues

4. grill-me

Section titled “4. grill-me”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/grill-me
  • What it does: Ruthlessly interrogates your proposal, walking through every branch of the decision tree until consensus
  • Core workflow:
    • One question at a time
    • Each question comes with a recommended answer
    • Questions answerable by exploring the codebase are answered by reading code, not asking you
  • Use cases:
    • Planning to split a monorepo into microservices but unsure about boundaries — let it grill you
    • Stress-testing any major technical decision
    • Running a “devil’s advocate” pass before writing an RFC

5. design-an-interface

Section titled “5. design-an-interface”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/design-an-interface
  • What it does: Based on John Ousterhout’s “Design It Twice” principle, uses parallel sub-agents to generate 3+ radically different interface designs, then compares them
  • Core workflow:
    1. Gather requirements (problem, callers, key operations, constraints)
    2. Launch 3+ parallel sub-agents, each with different constraints (minimalist, flexible, common-case optimized, etc.)
    3. Present each design (signatures, usage examples, hidden complexity)
    4. Multi-dimensional comparison (interface simplicity, generality, implementation efficiency, module depth)
    5. User selects or mixes
  • Use cases:
    • Designing cache module APIs, plugin systems, SDK interfaces, and other critical modules
    • Avoiding the “first idea is the final idea” trap

6. request-refactor-plan

Section titled “6. request-refactor-plan”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/request-refactor-plan
  • What it does: Generates a detailed refactoring plan through interviews, broken into tiny safe commits, submitted as a GitHub Issue
  • Core workflow:
    1. Gather problem description and initial proposal
    2. Explore codebase to verify
    3. Discuss alternatives
    4. Define precise scope (what changes, what doesn’t)
    5. Check test coverage
    6. Split commit plan following Martin Fowler’s “each step as small as possible” principle
    7. Create GitHub Issue (problem, solution, commit list, decision documentation)
  • Use cases:
    • Want to unify scattered state management to Zustand but afraid of breaking things
    • Any large-scale refactoring spanning multiple files and modules

II. Development

Section titled “II. Development”

7. tdd

Section titled “7. tdd”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/tdd
  • What it does: Strict red-green-refactor TDD cycles, progressing one vertical slice at a time
  • Core philosophy:
    • Tests verify behavior (through public interfaces), not implementation details
    • Horizontal slicing strictly forbidden (writing all tests before any code)
    • One test → one implementation → refactor → next (vertical slicing)
    • Good tests read like specifications and survive refactoring
  • Use cases:
    • Adding refund functionality to a payment module, progressing step by step
    • Writing a failing test before fixing a bug
    • Building TDD habits in AI agents

8. triage-issue

Section titled “8. triage-issue”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/triage-issue
  • What it does: Automatically investigates bug root causes, explores the codebase, generates GitHub Issues with TDD fix plans
  • Core workflow:
    1. Get problem description (asks only one question)
    2. Deep codebase exploration: locate bug, trace code paths, find root cause, check related code
    3. Determine fix approach (minimal changes)
    4. Design TDD fix plan (ordered RED-GREEN cycles)
    5. Create GitHub Issue
  • Use cases:
    • User reports “page occasionally goes blank” — nearly hands-free automatic investigation
    • Open-source issue triage, auto-generating fix proposals

9. improve-codebase-architecture

Section titled “9. improve-codebase-architecture”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/improve-codebase-architecture
  • What it does: Organically explores the codebase, discovers architectural improvement opportunities, focusing on deepening shallow modules and improving testability
  • Core concept: Deep Modules (John Ousterhout) = small interfaces hiding large implementations, more testable, more AI-friendly
  • Core workflow:
    1. Organically explore codebase, record friction points
    2. Present candidate improvements (coupling clusters, dependency types, test impact)
    3. User selects candidates
    4. Propose multiple refactoring approaches using design-an-interface methodology
    5. Create GitHub Issue RFC
  • Use cases:
    • Project growing large, small files everywhere with tangled dependencies, “something feels wrong but can’t articulate it”
    • Regular architecture health checks

10. migrate-to-shoehorn

Section titled “10. migrate-to-shoehorn”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/migrate-to-shoehorn
  • What it does: Migrates as type assertions in test files to @total-typescript/shoehorn
  • Migration patterns:
    • as Type → fromPartial() (passing partial data)
    • as unknown as Type → fromAny() (intentionally passing wrong data)
    • When large objects only care about a few properties, no more faking entire objects
  • Use cases:
    • TypeScript projects with as assertion sprawl in tests, wanting better type safety
    • Note: This is Matt Pocock’s own library, suited for the Total TypeScript ecosystem

11. scaffold-exercises

Section titled “11. scaffold-exercises”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/scaffold-exercises
  • What it does: Creates exercise directory structures for courses (section → exercise → problem/solution/explainer)
  • Core specs:
    • Section: XX-section-name/, Exercise: XX.YY-exercise-name/
    • Each exercise needs problem/, solution/, or explainer/ subdirectories
    • Auto-runs lint to verify correct structure
  • Use cases:
    • Batch-generating exercise scaffolding for TypeScript/programming tutorials
    • Note: Primarily for Matt’s Total TypeScript course system, limited general applicability

III. Tooling & Setup

Section titled “III. Tooling & Setup”

12. setup-pre-commit

Section titled “12. setup-pre-commit”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/setup-pre-commit
  • What it does: One-click setup of Husky + lint-staged + Prettier pre-commit hooks
  • Core workflow:
    1. Detect package manager (npm/pnpm/yarn/bun)
    2. Install husky, lint-staged, prettier
    3. Initialize Husky, create .husky/pre-commit
    4. Configure lint-staged (Prettier formatting)
    5. Optionally add typecheck and test
    6. Verify + commit
  • Use cases:
    • Setting up commit hooks in one step when initializing new projects
    • Adding code quality gates to existing projects

13. git-guardrails-claude-code

Section titled “13. git-guardrails-claude-code”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/git-guardrails-claude-code
  • What it does: Sets up PreToolUse hooks for Claude Code to intercept dangerous git commands
  • Intercepts: git push (including —force), git reset --hard, git clean -f, git branch -D, git checkout .
  • Scope: Project-level (.claude/settings.json) or global (~/.claude/settings.json)
  • Use cases:
    • Letting Claude Code write code autonomously while preventing pushes or destructive operations
    • Security measure specifically for Claude Code

IV. Writing & Knowledge

Section titled “IV. Writing & Knowledge”

14. write-a-skill

Section titled “14. write-a-skill”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/write-a-skill
  • What it does: Teaches you to create new agent skills with proper structure, progressive disclosure, and resource bundling
  • Skill structure:
  • Key point: The description is the sole basis for an agent deciding whether to load a skill — it must be precise
  • Use cases:
    • Creating custom “code review”, “deployment workflow” skills for your team
    • The meta-skill — a skill for making skills

15. edit-article

Section titled “15. edit-article”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/edit-article
  • What it does: Edits and improves articles — reorders sections by information dependency, rewrites each section for clarity
  • Core workflow:
    1. Split into sections by headings, analyze information dependencies (DAG)
    2. Confirm section order
    3. Rewrite each section, max 240 characters per paragraph
  • Use cases:
    • Blog drafts with loose structure needing professional editing
    • Technical documentation review and improvement

16. ubiquitous-language

Section titled “16. ubiquitous-language”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/ubiquitous-language
  • What it does: Extracts DDD-style ubiquitous language glossaries from conversations, flags ambiguities/synonyms, outputs UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md
  • Output format: Domain-grouped terminology tables (term, definition, aliases to avoid) + entity relationships + example conversations
  • Use cases:
    • Team discussions where “user/customer/account” are used interchangeably, needing unified terminology
    • First step in building domain models when starting new projects
    • A DDD practitioner’s power tool

17. obsidian-vault

Section titled “17. obsidian-vault”
  • Install: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/obsidian-vault
  • What it does: Searches, creates, and manages notes in an Obsidian vault, supporting wikilinks and index notes
  • Features: Search by filename/content, create Title Case notes, auto-add wikilinks, find backlinks, maintain index pages
  • Use cases:
    • Let AI help organize and link notes in Obsidian
    • Note: Vault path is hardcoded to Matt’s location, modify before use

V. Universality Ratings

Section titled “V. Universality Ratings”
RatingSkillsNotes
⭐⭐⭐ Universalwrite-a-prd, prd-to-plan, grill-me, design-an-interface, tdd, edit-article, ubiquitous-languageAny project, any team benefits immediately
⭐⭐ Workflow-specificprd-to-issues, triage-issue, improve-codebase-architecture, request-refactor-plan, setup-pre-commit, write-a-skillRequires GitHub Issues workflow or specific scenarios
⭐ Personal/Nichemigrate-to-shoehorn, scaffold-exercises, git-guardrails-claude-code, obsidian-vaultTightly coupled to Matt’s personal toolchain

VI. Design Philosophy Summary

Section titled “VI. Design Philosophy Summary”

Matt Pocock’s skills system is built on several core principles:

  1. Vertical Slicing (Tracer Bullet) — Threading through the complete chain of write-a-prd → prd-to-plan → prd-to-issues → tdd, every step emphasizes end-to-end thin slices over horizontal layering
  2. Deep Modules — From John Ousterhout’s A Philosophy of Software Design, small interfaces hiding large implementations, central to design-an-interface and improve-codebase-architecture
  3. Design It Twice — Don’t fall in love with your first design; explore multiple approaches in parallel
  4. Tiny Commits — Martin Fowler’s refactoring philosophy, keeping code runnable at every step
  5. Behavior Tests Over Implementation Tests — The core of the TDD skill; tests should read like specifications and survive refactoring

Recommended combination path: grill-me → write-a-prd → design-an-interface → prd-to-plan → prd-to-issues → tdd

Release date: 2026-04-07 | 18 new features in total

1. CLI/infer — Unified Inference Hub

Section titled “1. CLI/infer — Unified Inference Hub”

New openclaw infer ... top-level command unifies model inference, media generation, web scraping, and embeddings under a single CLI hub. Previously, invoking different provider capabilities required scattered subcommands. openclaw infer consolidates all provider-backed inference workflows into one command family.

2. Tools/Media Generation — Smart Fallback & Parameter Adaptation

Section titled “2. Tools/Media Generation — Smart Fallback & Parameter Adaptation”

Media generation tools now support cross-provider auto-fallback, intent preservation, smart parameter mapping, and video-to-video mode awareness. When the preferred provider is unavailable, the system seamlessly switches to alternatives while remapping parameters to the closest match.

3. Memory/Wiki — Structured Knowledge Base Returns

Section titled “3. Memory/Wiki — Structured Knowledge Base Returns”

Restored and enhanced built-in memory-wiki stack with claim/evidence structure, contradiction detection, staleness dashboard, and freshness-weighted search. Enterprise-grade features for long-term agent memory management.

4. Plugins/Webhooks — Webhook Ingress Plugin

New built-in webhook ingress plugin allows external automations to create and drive bound TaskFlows through HTTP endpoints with shared secrets. Standardized routing and security model for CI/CD, monitoring, and third-party SaaS integrations.

5. Gateway/Sessions — Compaction Checkpoints with Branch & Restore

Section titled “5. Gateway/Sessions — Compaction Checkpoints with Branch & Restore”

Persistent compaction checkpoints with Sessions UI branch and restore operations. Makes compaction reversible — critical for debugging, auditing, and recovering lost context.

6. Compaction — Pluggable Compaction Providers

Section titled “6. Compaction — Pluggable Compaction Providers”

Fully pluggable compaction provider registry allowing plugins to replace the built-in LLM summary pipeline. Use cheaper models, preserve code blocks, or implement rule-based extraction.

7. Agents/System Prompt — Override & Heartbeat Prompt Control

Section titled “7. Agents/System Prompt — Override & Heartbeat Prompt Control”

New systemPromptOverride for controlled A/B prompt experiments, plus heartbeat prompt section control to reduce token waste while keeping heartbeat runtime behavior active.

8. Providers/Google — Gemma 4 Support

Section titled “8. Providers/Google — Gemma 4 Support”

Added Gemma 4 model support with fixed fallback resolution on Google provider paths, restoring native Gemma routing.

9. Providers/Google — Gemma 4 Thinking Semantics

Section titled “9. Providers/Google — Gemma 4 Thinking Semantics”

Preserves Gemma 4’s explicit thinking-off semantics while enabling reasoning support in the compatibility wrapper. Fine-grained thinking mode control.

10. Providers/Arcee AI — New Arcee AI Provider

Section titled “10. Providers/Arcee AI — New Arcee AI Provider”

New first-class Arcee AI provider with Trinity model catalog, OpenRouter support, and guided onboarding.

11. Providers/Anthropic — Claude CLI Restored as Preferred Local Path

Section titled “11. Providers/Anthropic — Claude CLI Restored as Preferred Local Path”

Claude CLI restored as the preferred local Anthropic access method across onboarding, doctor checks, and Docker scenarios.

12. Providers/Ollama — Vision Capability Auto-Detection

Redacted session transcripts now ingested into the dreaming corpus for richer offline memory consolidation with cursor checkpoints for incremental processing.

Section titled “14. Providers/inferrs — Strict OpenAI-Compatible Backend Support”

String-content compatibility for stricter OpenAI-compatible backends, with full inferrs configuration examples and troubleshooting guides.

Section titled “15. Agents/Context Engine — Prompt Cache Runtime Exposure”

Prompt-cache runtime context exposed to the context engine, ensuring accurate cache statistics for optimized prompt assembly.

Section titled “16. Plugin SDK/Context Engines — assemble() Enhancement”

availableTools, citationsMode, and memory seams now passed to assemble(), enabling companion plugins to consume active memory state through formal APIs.

Section titled “17. ACP/ACPX Plugin — ACPX 0.5.1 Upgrade”

Built-in ACPX pin bumped to 0.5.1 for latest runtime compatibility.

Guide to Enabling OpenClaw Dreaming (Experimental)

Apr 6, 2026
Vibe Sparking

What Is Dreaming

Section titled “What Is Dreaming”

Dreaming is the background memory consolidation system built into OpenClaw’s memory-core plugin. It mimics how human sleep consolidates memories — automatically promoting high-frequency, high-relevance short-term memories into persistent long-term memory (written to MEMORY.md).

The feature is disabled by default and must be enabled manually.

The Three Phases of Dreaming

Section titled “The Three Phases of Dreaming”

Each sweep executes three phases in order:

PhasePurposeWrites to MEMORY.md
LightIngests recent short-term memory signals, deduplicates and stages candidate entries❌
REMExtracts thematic and reflective signals, providing enhanced scoring for the Deep phase❌
DeepWeighted scoring, promotes qualifying candidates to MEMORY.md✅

Deep Phase Scoring Weights

Section titled “Deep Phase Scoring Weights”
SignalWeightDescription
Frequency0.24Short-term signal accumulation count
Relevance0.30Average retrieval quality
Query diversity0.15Number of distinct queries/day contexts that triggered the signal
Recency0.15Time-decay freshness
Consolidation0.10Cross-day recurrence strength
Conceptual richness0.06Concept tag density

Promotion thresholds: minScore >= 0.8, minRecallCount >= 3, minUniqueQueries >= 3

Dreaming Output Files

Section titled “Dreaming Output Files”
  • Machine state: memory/.dreams/ (recall store, phase signals, ingestion checkpoints, locks)
  • Human-readable: DREAMS.md (or existing dreams.md), containing phase summaries and a Dream Diary
  • Phase reports (optional): memory/dreaming/<phase>/YYYY-MM-DD.md
  • Long-term memory: Only the Deep phase writes to MEMORY.md

How to Enable It

Section titled “How to Enable It”

1. Edit openclaw.json

Section titled “1. Edit openclaw.json”

Add the memory-core configuration under plugins.entries:

memory-core is a built-in plugin — no installation needed, just declare it in your config.

To modify via command line:

2. Restart the Gateway

Section titled “2. Restart the Gateway”

3. Verify

Section titled “3. Verify”

After restarting, memory-core will automatically create a cron job to schedule dreaming sweeps. Confirm via cron list:

You should see a job named “Memory Dreaming Promotion” with these defaults:

  • Schedule: 0 3 * * * (daily at UTC 03:00)
  • Session Target: main session
  • Payload: systemEvent
  • Wake Mode: next-heartbeat

Optional Configuration

Section titled “Optional Configuration”

Adjusting Sweep Frequency

Section titled “Adjusting Sweep Frequency”

frequency accepts a standard cron expression; the default is 0 3 * * *.

Configuration Reference

Section titled “Configuration Reference”
SettingDefaultDescription
dreaming.enabledfalseWhether to enable dreaming
dreaming.frequency0 3 * * *Sweep schedule (cron expression)

Promotion thresholds (minScore, minRecallCount, minUniqueQueries) are managed internally by memory-core and cannot currently be adjusted via configuration.

Hands-On Walkthrough

Section titled “Hands-On Walkthrough”

This setup was completed entirely within an OpenClaw agent’s main session:

  1. Confirmed the current config had no memory-core entry under plugins.entries
  2. Used a Python script to inject memory-core.config.dreaming.enabled: true into the config file
  3. Ran openclaw gateway restart — service restarted successfully
  4. Verified via cron list that memory-core automatically created the “Memory Dreaming Promotion” cron job
  5. Confirmed job parameters: 0 3 * * *, main session, systemEvent

The entire process took about 2 minutes with no additional plugins to install.
